title: Serotonin: Where Does It Go?
description: Interactive body map that traces serotonin released by enterochromaffin cells in the gut lining: it acts on nerves, is taken back up by the serotonin transporter, or is stored in platelets, but it cannot cross the blood-brain barrier. Tryptophan from food can cross, and brain neurons turn it into their own serotonin. An SSRI checkbox shows how blocking the serotonin transporter changes gut serotonin, a source of common side effects.
creator: Aaryav Sharma
subject: neuroscience (gut-brain axis)
publisher: Gut Check: The Neuroscience of How Your Gut and Brain Talk
learningObjectives: Distinguish gut (peripheral) serotonin from brain (central) serotonin by tracing the fates of serotonin released by enterochromaffin cells.
Explain why gut serotonin cannot raise brain serotonin and how the brain makes its own serotonin from tryptophan.
Explain why an SSRI can cause gastrointestinal side effects.
prerequisites: A neurotransmitter is a chemical messenger released by neurons
The vagus nerve carries signals from the gut to the brainstem
keyQuestions: Where does serotonin made in the gut go?
Why can't gut serotonin cross into the brain?
How does the brain make its own serotonin?
Why can a medicine aimed at the brain upset the stomach?
misconceptions: Serotonin made in the gut travels to the brain and improves mood.
Eating foods that contain serotonin raises brain serotonin.
A nerve signal from the gut means serotonin itself reached the brain.
Most tryptophan from food becomes serotonin.
